clinicalPearls: Influenza presents with an abrupt febrile illness: fever, myalgias, fatigue, sore throat, headache, and cough (Harrison 22e p.1576).

Influenza A viruses are the most virulent for humans and cause most severe disease, though type B viruses (Victoria lineage) also cause substantial morbidity; type A is subdivided by hemagglutinin (H) and neuraminidase (N) surface protein subtypes (Harrison 22e p.1576).
Two type A subtypes (H1N1 and H3N2) and one type B lineage (Victoria) cause annual seasonal epidemics, which occur in winter in temperate regions (Harrison 22e p.1576, p.1579).

Influenza pneumonia has an unusually high rate of complication by bacterial superinfection, with staphylococcal and streptococcal pneumonia occurring in as many as 10% of cases in some series (Harrison 22e p.1576).

Antiviral treatment of influenza is effective only when given early in the course of illness; baloxavir marboxil is approved for acute uncomplicated flu when started within 2 days of onset (Harrison 22e p.1537, p.1580).

Antibiotics do NOT improve the outcome of uncomplicated viral respiratory infection in otherwise healthy people, but influenza can be complicated by secondary bacterial infection that does warrant antibacterials (Harrison 22e p.1537).

Annual vaccine reformulation is required because antigenic drift (point mutations in HA and NA) causes antigenic divergence; an occasional antigenic mismatch can render a vaccine component of negligible efficacy (Harrison 22e p.1538).
harrison.pathophysiology: Influenza is a single-stranded, segmented, negative-sense RNA genome virus of the family Orthomyxoviridae, with four (sero)types: A, B, C, and D. Influenza A and C infect multiple species; B infects humans almost exclusively; D primarily infects cattle and is not known to infect humans. Influenza A is subdivided into 18 hemagglutinin (H) and 11 neuraminidase (N) surface-protein subtypes. Two distinct mechanisms drive antigenic variation: antigenic drift (accumulation of point mutations in the HA and NA molecules) produces the gradual divergence underlying annual epidemics and requires new vaccines each year; antigenic shift, enabled by the segmented genome allowing reassortment between two viruses co-infecting one host, can produce a major novel virus and a pandemic. Type B viruses mutate less frequently than type A, probably reflecting their near-exclusive human host range. Many highly pathogenic strains circulate in aquatic birds; pigs, which carry both avian and human receptors, can serve as a mixing vessel for reassortment that makes zoonotic viruses more fit for human replication (Harrison 22e p.1576).

Severe or fatal primary viral pneumonia, particularly in elderly patients, nursing-home residents, immunocompromised persons, and very young children
Hypoxia or respiratory failure requiring supplemental oxygen or mechanical ventilation

harrison.prognosis: Uncomplicated influenza in otherwise healthy adults is generally self-limited, and antiviral therapy started early shortens illness. Severe and even fatal pneumonia occurs particularly in elderly patients, nursing-home residents, immunocompromised persons, and very young children. Bacterial superinfection complicates as many as 10% of influenza pneumonia cases in some series. Pandemics caused by novel viruses occur on average every 20-30 years (Harrison 22e p.1576, p.1538).
pitfalls: RT-PCR is extremely sensitive: viral genome can persist in nasal secretions for weeks after an infection resolves, so a positive test may reflect a recently resolved rather than a currently acute infection, and laboratory contamination can produce false positives (Harrison 22e p.1537).
Rapid diagnostic tests have the highest positive predictive value when applied to high-risk, appropriately seasonal samples; indiscriminate testing lowers predictive value (Harrison 22e p.1537).
Adamantanes (amantadine, rimantadine) should not be relied upon: widespread resistance has occurred in many currently circulating influenza A viruses (Harrison 22e p.1580).
Antiviral therapy started late is of limited benefit, as it is effective mainly when given early in the course (Harrison 22e p.1537).
management: Start antiviral therapy early with neuraminidase inhibitors (oseltamivir or zanamivir) or the endonuclease inhibitor baloxavir marboxil, prioritising high-risk and hospitalised patients
Provide supportive care with antipyretics, analgesia, hydration and oxygen as needed, avoiding antibacterials for uncomplicated viral illness
Treat secondary bacterial pneumonia with antibacterials directed at staphylococcal and streptococcal superinfection
Prevent disease and spread with annual inactivated influenza vaccination and antiviral post-exposure prophylaxis for vulnerable contacts
Monitor high-risk groups (the elderly, immunocompromised, very young and those with comorbidities) for deterioration and complications
Escalate to hospital admission and respiratory support for severe or complicated pneumonia and respiratory failure
